# Purpose

`build_contrast_analysis()` chains three steps:

1. a **strategy** says which model to fit per protein, e.g. `strategy_lm()`
2. `build_model()` fits it to every protein and returns a `Model`
3. `Contrasts` computes the contrasts from the models; `ContrastsModerated` shrinks their variances with the empirical Bayes method

This article runs the steps by hand for the `lm` method. Use them to inspect the per-protein models, to change one step, or to add a new modelling backend. For analyses, use `build_contrast_analysis()`.

```{r data}
library(prolfqua)
sim <- sim_lfq_data_protein_config(Nprot = 100, seed = 1234)
lfq <- LFQData$new(sim$data, sim$config)
contrasts <- c(AvsC = "group_A - group_Ctrl", BvsC = "group_B - group_Ctrl")
```

# The facade

```{r facade}
fa <- build_contrast_analysis(lfq, "~ group_", contrasts, method = "lm")
```

# The same, step by step

The `lm` method weights each protein intensity by its number of peptides, the column `lfq$nr_children_col()`.

```{r steps}
strat <- strategy_lm(paste(lfq$response(), "~ group_"), weights = lfq$nr_children_col())
mod <- build_model(lfq, strat)
contr <- Contrasts$new(mod, contrasts, model_name = "lm")
contr_mod <- ContrastsModerated$new(contr)
```

Both give the same result:

```{r same}
by_facade <- dplyr::arrange(fa$get_contrasts(), protein_Id, contrast)
by_hand <- dplyr::arrange(contr_mod$get_contrasts(), protein_Id, contrast)
all.equal(by_facade$diff, by_hand$diff)
all.equal(by_facade$p.value, by_hand$p.value)
```

The facade keeps the intermediate objects, so you can also take them from there: `fa$model` is the `Model`, `fa$contrast` the moderated contrasts.

# Inspecting the models

`mod$model_df` holds one row per protein with its fitted model and fit diagnostics.

```{r modelDf}
mod$model_df |>
  dplyr::select(protein_Id, has_model_fit, isSingular, nr_coef_not_NA, sigma, df.residual) |>
  head()
```

The analysis of variance per protein, and the distribution of its FDR:

```{r anova, fig.cap = "FDR of the per-protein analysis of variance."}
head(mod$get_anova())
mod$anova_histogram("FDR")$plot
```

The model coefficients:

```{r coefficients}
head(mod$get_coefficients())
```

# From a formula to coefficient weights

`setup_analysis()` treats configured predictors as categorical labels. It converts numeric predictors and ordered factors to character too, so ordered levels and numeric slopes are not retained by that route. It builds the configured identifiers and retains the analysis columns; other columns and their attributes are discarded. The names in `config$factors` are the predictor names used in the formula. Method keys, predictor names and contrast names are case sensitive.

R normally uses treatment coding (`options("contrasts")`): an intercept for the reference group and one coefficient per other level. When predictors are character labels, the first sorted level is normally the reference. In this small example we explicitly set `Ctrl` as the reference to make the coefficients easy to read:

```{r design-one-factor}
one_factor <- data.frame(
  group_ = factor(rep(c("Ctrl", "A", "B"), each = 3), levels = c("Ctrl", "A", "B")),
  abundance = c(19.8, 20, 20.2, 21.8, 22, 22.2, 18.8, 19, 19.2)
)
one_model <- lm(abundance ~ group_, data = one_factor)
unique(model.matrix(one_model))
coef(one_model)
```

The coefficient vector is `(Intercept)`, `group_A`, `group_B`: control abundance, A minus control, and B minus control. `linfct_from_model()` represents each group mean as a row of weights on those coefficients. Internally `.model_coeff_matrix()` creates the weights for observed factor combinations and `.coeff_weights_factor_levels()` averages them equally within each factor level. `linfct_matrix_contrasts()` then evaluates the named expression using those group rows:

```{r one-factor-weights}
one_means <- linfct_from_model(one_model)$linfct_factors
one_means
one_contrast <- linfct_matrix_contrasts(one_means, c(A_vs_Ctrl = "group_A - group_Ctrl"))
one_contrast
drop(one_contrast %*% coef(one_model))
```

Here `A_vs_Ctrl` has weights `(0, 1, 0)` and estimates a difference of 2. If A were the reference, the individual coefficient names and weights would change, but the same contrast of group means would still estimate A minus control. The contrast strings refer to group means, which should not be confused with individual treatment-coded coefficients.

## Two factors and their interaction

`~ A * B` expands to `~ A + B + A:B`. With two levels per factor, its four columns are an intercept, the A effect at the B reference level, the B effect at the A reference level, and their interaction. The interaction is the change in the A effect between the two B levels:

```{r design-interaction}
two_factor <- expand.grid(A = c("a0", "a1"), B = c("b0", "b1"), replicate = 1:3)
two_factor$abundance <- 20 + 3 * (two_factor$A == "a1") - 2 * (two_factor$B == "b1") +
  4 * (two_factor$A == "a1" & two_factor$B == "b1") + rep(c(-0.2, 0, 0.2), each = 4)
two_model <- lm(abundance ~ A * B, data = two_factor)
unique(model.matrix(two_model))
coef(two_model)
```

Cell means include the corresponding intercept, main effects and interaction. Quote the cell names with backticks because they contain colons. A main-effect row in `linfct_factors` averages equally over the observed cells containing that factor level; a row in `linfct_interactions` describes one cell. In this balanced example, the marginal A difference is 5, the A difference at `b0` is 3, and the difference at `b1` is 7:

```{r interaction-weights}
two_means <- linfct_from_model(two_model)
two_means$linfct_factors
two_means$linfct_interactions
two_weights <- linfct_matrix_contrasts(
  linfct_from_model(two_model, as_list = FALSE),
  c(
    A_marginal = "Aa1 - Aa0",
    A_at_b0 = "`Aa1:Bb0` - `Aa0:Bb0`",
    A_at_b1 = "`Aa1:Bb1` - `Aa0:Bb1`",
    A_by_B = "A_at_b1 - A_at_b0"
  )
)
two_weights
drop(two_weights %*% coef(two_model))
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(drop(two_weights %*% coef(two_model))), c(5, 3, 7, 4)))
```

These helpers assume categorical predictors and the usual intercept-based coding. They do not implement general marginal means for continuous covariates or arbitrary contrast coding. Missing factor combinations can make some rows unestimable; unavailable groups in the contrast expressions are reported by a warning at the low-level interface, and the facade rejects a group absent from the entire dataset.

# Without moderation

`Contrasts` alone gives the unmoderated contrasts, which the facades do not expose. Moderation stabilises the variances estimated from few observations:

```{r moderation}
data.frame(
  contrasts = c("Contrasts", "ContrastsModerated"),
  FDR_lt_0.1 = c(
    sum(contr$get_contrasts()$FDR < 0.1, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(contr_mod$get_contrasts()$FDR < 0.1, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)
```

# Changing one step

Replace the strategy to fit another model per protein, e.g. a robust linear model with `strategy_rlm()`; the other steps stay the same.

```{r rlm}
mod_rlm <- build_model(lfq, strategy_rlm(paste(lfq$response(), "~ group_")))
contr_rlm <- ContrastsModerated$new(Contrasts$new(mod_rlm, contrasts, model_name = "rlm"))
head(contr_rlm$get_contrasts()[, c("protein_Id", "contrast", "diff", "p.value", "FDR")])
```

# Adding a backend

A facade class wraps the steps of one method. `register_facade()` adds it to the registry, after which `build_contrast_analysis(method = ...)` finds it. `list_facades()` shows the registry:

```{r registry}
names(list_facades())
```
